---------------------------------------------SUBJECTIVE------------------------------------------

   1. Active immunization vaccines?

It is the induction of immunity after exposure of host to antigen. In this case, antigenic
exposure is mandatory. Active immunization can occur naturally by exposing to microbe
or other antigen when there is no prior exposure before the entry of antigen. Similarly
there is also no pre made antibodies in the host’s serum. In this form of immunization,
immune system develops antibodies against the microbe after its exposure. This process
of antibodies generation is considered slow. Moreover a memory response is also
generated in which antibodies remained in use for longer time. This form of
immunization can be artificial in nature which is achieved by either injection of microbe
before natural exposure or treated microbes or toxins

   2. Opsonization?

It is the process by which phagocytosis of microbes by immune cells get enhanced. Those
proteins which undertake this process are called as opsonins. For example, some
complement proteins like C3b, iC3b and C4b are good opsonins. These proteins attach to
microorganism first making a complex. This complex of complement protein & microbe
bind with complement receptor on the surface of phagocytic cell as a result phagocytosis
of microbe occur by phagocytes

Q1. Functions of Cytokines?                  5 Marks
• Used as biological response modifier for treatment of various diseases
• Cytokine is a general term but more specific term used according to their cell of origin
• Monokines: produced by mononuclear phagocytic cells
• Lymphokines: produced by activated lymphocytes
Cytokines function as cascade signaling in the form of cytokine network
Cytokines are considered as redundant
• Redundancy: is due to the nature of cytokine receptors

Q2. Subregion of variable region of antibody?                        5 Marks
Variable region
• Present on heavy & light chains of Immunoglobulins
Two sub-regions
1) Hypervariable (HVR)
• Based on variability of amino acid sequences
• Complementarity determining region
2) Framework Regions
• Regions between hypervariable regions
• Groups & sub-groups of immunoglobulins
• Products of different variable region genes

Q3. Types of Autoimmunity?                      2 Marks
Autoimmunity:
Classification based on tissues or organs involved
• Two following categories

Effort By Amaan Khan

• Organ-specific autoimmunity
• Non-organ Specific autoimmunity

Q4. Effector Function of complement protein?                   3 Marks
Effector Functions of Complement Proteins
• Opsonization (Opsonins)
• Chemoattraction (Chemoattractants)
• Anaphylaxsis (Anaphylatoxins)
• Pro-Inflammatory

Q5. Primary and secondary antibody response?                  2 Marks
Primary Ab response
• First kind of antibody response against antigen
• Major class of antibody is IgM
• Ab are with less affinity & less persistent
Secondary Ab response
• Second kind of antibody response against antigen
• Major class is IgG but may IgE or IgA but less IgM

Q6. Inflammation and its role in body?                  3 Marks
Inflammation is the body’s attempt: To protect the body from harmful stimulus. Complex Tissue
response
• Part of body’s immune system
• Inflammatory response: series of events for inflammation
• For wound healing
• For clearance of infections

Q7. What is Opsonization?                   2 Marks

Effort By Amaan Khan

Opsonization: some complement proteins are good opsonins. C3b, iC3b and C4b attach to
microorganism first. This complex of complement protein binds with complement receptor on
the surface of phagocytic cell. Phagocytosis of microbe.

Q8. Write two main types of tumor associated antigens.                      2 Marks
• There are two main types of tumor associated antigens
1) Tumor specific transplantation antigens
2) Tumor Associated transplantation antigens

Q9. Differentiate between Organ Specific autoimmunity and Non-Organ
Specific autoimmunity. 2 Marks
Organ Specific autoimmunity
• Immune response against organ associated specific antigens
• Antibodies against organ associated antigens damage the organ
• Target organs
• Skin
• Thyroid gland
• Muscles
Non-Organ Specific autoimmunity
• Immune response not against organ associated specific antigens
• Antibodies against not organ associated antigens
• Systemic autoimmune diseases
• Mainly target organs: skin, joints, soft tissues etc.

Q10. Write down the mechanism of Oxygen independent killing?                        3
Marks
1) Oxygen Independent
• No need of oxygen for such kind of intracellular killing of bacteria
• Granules & Vesicles of phagocytes secrete hydrolytic proteins

Effort By Amaan Khan

• Those proteins are bacteriocidal in nature according to their modes of action
Effector Molecule Function:
Cationic proteins (including cathepsin): Damage to microbial membranes
Lysozyme: Splits mucopeptide in bacterial cell wall
Lactoferrin: Deprives proliferating bacteria of iron
Proteolytic and hydrolytic enzymes: Digestion of killed organisms

Q11. How the fragment of antibodies is obtained? Briefly elucide the
properties of the fragment?    5 Marks
Antibodies Fragments
• Produced by proteolytic enzymes i.e papain
• Two fragments are produced which have structure & function relationship
1) Fab
2) Fc

1) Fab
• Fragment for antigen binding (Fab)
• Papain causes the cleavage at hinge regions to produce two identical fragments containing one
heavy & one light chain
• Having monovalent valency for antigen binding
2) Fc
• Crystalizable Fragment (Fc)
• Contain two heavy chains with CH2 & CH3 domains
• Performed effector functions

Q12. Applications of Agglutination reaction?                     2 Marks
Applications of Agglutination
• Blood grouping: ABO & Rh for both either on the basis of antigens of RBC or antibodies of
serum
• Assessing bacterial infections e.g Widal test for diagnosis of Typhoid fever

Effort By Amaan Khan

Q13. Tolerance is achieved by natural and artificial?                       2 Marks
Naturally: In case of autoimmune disorders e.g Rheumatoid Arthritis, SLE etc.
2) Artificially: exposure to immunosuppressive drugs or X-ray irradiation e.g in case of
experimental animals for bone marrow transplantation

Q14. Usage of Monoclonal antibodies?                      3 Marks
• Usage in prevention, diagnosis & treatment of disease
• Immunophenotyping of Immune cells: Monoclonal Ab used against cell surface molecules like
Cluster of Differentiation (CD)
• Typing of various tumors e.g Leukemia • Immunohistochemistry of solid tumors
• Use in Immunotherapy: Against various tumor marker e.g CD20 B-Cell lymphoma
• Use in Fluorescence Activated cell sorting (FACS)

Q15. Cytokines in adaptive immune system?                           5 Marks
• Cytokines which act primarily for Adaptive (Specific) immune system
1) IL-2
• Produced by Th cells but Tc also produced in lesser extent
• Stimulate B-cell division Can also activate NK cells s& monocytes
• IL-2 acts in autocrine manner on T-cells
• Activation of T-cells result in expression of IL2R & production of IL-2
• IL-2 binds to IL-2R and promotes cell division
• IL-2R decay if T-cells are not activated & eventually proliferative phase ends
2) IL-4
• IL-4 is produced by
macrophages &Th2 cells

Immune system is the defense system that has evolved to protect animals from invading
pathogenic microorganisms and cancer.
It is able to generate an enormous variety of cells and molecules capable of specifically

Immune response
An immune response can be divided into two related activities

Recognition
Response
Immune recognition is remarkable for its specificity. The immune system is able to recognize
subtle chemical differences that distinguish one foreign pathogen from another.
Furthermore, the system is able to discriminate between foreign molecules and the body’s own cells and
proteins.
Once a foreign organism has been recognized, the immune system recruits a variety of cells and
molecules to mount an appropriate response, called an effector response, to eliminate or
neutralize the organism.

Non-infectious disease
Non-infectious diseases are not caused by pathogens and therefore cannot be spread from
one person to another. Instead, non-infectious diseases are caused by factors such as
genetics, malnutrition, environment and lifestyle.

Disease: Typhoid Fever

     A few years ago, I was diagnosed with typhoid after experiencing a constant high fever,
      weakness, and stomach pain for several days.
     I think my immune system's first response was inflammation—my body raised the
      temperature to slow down the growth of Salmonella Typhi bacteria.
     I had no appetite and felt extremely weak. I believe this was my body saving energy to
      fuel the immune cells like neutrophils and macrophages, which were likely fighting the
      infection.
     My doctor explained that typhoid affects the intestines, so I assumed my gut-associated
      immune tissues (like Peyer's patches) were actively involved in recognizing and fighting
      the bacteria.
     I was given antibiotics, but I noticed improvement only after a few days. I believe my
      adaptive immunity was also building up, producing specific antibodies against the
      bacteria.
     During recovery, I had night sweats and felt thirsty often, which I think was my body's
      way of flushing out toxins and dead bacterial cells.
     I rested for almost two weeks, allowing my immune system to fully clear the infection
      and repair damaged tissues.
     Since then, I’ve become more cautious with food hygiene, but I also believe that my
      immune memory cells help protect me if I ever get exposed again.
     Looking back, I realize how amazing it is that our body has layers of defense—from
      quick responders like white blood cells to more targeted responses through antibodies.
     This experience taught me that even though medicines help, it’s our immune system that
      does the real long-term work of protecting and healing us.

Solution IDEA
Personal Experience: Dengue Fever and My Body’s Immune Response
1. Disease Overview
     A few years ago, I was diagnosed with Dengue Fever, a viral disease
      transmitted by the bite of Aedes mosquitoes.
     The illness began with a sudden high fever, severe joint and muscle pain,
      headache, and rash.
     A blood test confirmed the presence of the dengue virus, and my platelet
      count had dropped significantly.

2. Innate Immune Response (First Line of Defense)
     My innate immune system responded as soon as the virus entered my
      body. This is the body’s non-specific defense.
     Symptoms like fever, body aches, and inflammation were signs that the
      immune system was fighting the virus.
     White blood cells like neutrophils and macrophages tried to destroy the
      virus particles and infected cells.
     Though this response was fast, it was not specialized to the dengue virus.

3. Adaptive Immune Response (Specific Defense)
     After a few days, my adaptive immune system activated, which targets
      specific viruses.
     B cells identified the dengue virus and started producing antibodies to
      neutralize it.
     T-helper cells supported the B cells, and cytotoxic T cells attacked
      infected body cells directly.
     This phase was crucial for clearing the virus from my body.

4. Antibody Production and Immunological Memory
       The first type of antibodies produced were IgM, which are short-lived
        and appear early during infection.
       Later, IgG antibodies developed, providing longer-term protection.
       The body also created memory B and T cells that would help in
        recognizing the virus if I ever got infected again.
       However, with dengue, getting infected with a different strain later can
        cause severe reactions due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).

5. Monitoring and Recovery (Platelet Count and Fever Progression)
Day Platelet Count (per µL) Fever             Condition
1       210,000                     104°F     Onset of symptoms
3       140,000                     102°F     Hospital admission
5       90,000                      100°F     Weakness, close monitoring
7       130,000                     Normal Immune system improving
10      180,000                     Normal Discharged and recovering
       A drop in platelet count is a typical indicator of dengue infection.
       Recovery began as my immune response started controlling the infection,
        and my platelet levels slowly returned to normal.

6. Cytokine Response and Side Effects
       During infection, my immune cells released cytokines, which are
        chemical messengers that help coordinate the response.
       These cytokines called more immune cells to the infected areas and
        helped in clearing the virus.
       However, excessive cytokine release can be harmful and may lead to a
        condition called cytokine storm, which doctors closely monitored.

7. Supportive Treatment Helped the Immune System

      There is no specific antiviral medicine for dengue, so treatment focused
       on:
          o   Hydration (to prevent complications).
          o   Paracetamol (to reduce fever and pain).
          o   Complete rest (to allow the immune system to work effectively).
      These supportive measures gave my immune system time and strength to
       overcome the virus.

8. Chart: Phases of Dengue and Immune Response
Here is a simple chart showing how the body responds during different stages of
dengue infection:
 Phase               Timeline Immune Activity
 Febrile Phase       Day 1–3      Innate immunity starts (fever, WBCs)
 Critical Phase      Day 4–6      Low platelets, adaptive immunity begins
 Recovery Phase Day 7–10 Antibodies peak, memory cells formed

9. Lessons Learned from the Experience
      The human immune system has two powerful lines of defense: one that
       acts quickly and another that is highly specific.
      Although I recovered fully, I learned that dengue can be more dangerous
       upon reinfection due to complex immune mechanisms.
      I now take precautions like using mosquito repellents, removing stagnant
       water, and wearing protective clothing during dengue seasons.

•   ❖ My experience with nasal sinusitis began unexpectedly, during a cold and dusty
    season. What started as a simple flu quickly turned into something much worse — lasting
    congestion, intense facial pressure, and a flu that just wouldn’t go away. My nose was
    constantly irritated, and I experienced frequent episodes of blood and pus whenever I tried
    to clear it. The pain extended across my forehead and around my eyes, and no over-the-
    counter treatment seemed to help.

    gastroscopy. Through this procedure, he identified inflamed nasal polyps deep in my
    nasal cavity. These growths were blocking drainage pathways and were the main reason
    the infection was not resolving. To treat this locally, he administered long syringed
    injections directly into the polyps — a targeted and slightly painful approach, but
    necessary for shrinking the polyps and reducing inflammation. Along with this, he
    prescribed antibiotic nasal sprays and oral medications.
•   ❖ During this time, I could clearly feel my immune system fighting back. My body
    reacted with a high-grade fever, fatigue, and overall discomfort. These symptoms were
    not signs of weakness, but evidence that my immune system was in action. The presence
    of pus and blood discharge also confirmed that white blood cells like neutrophils were
    battling the infection deep within my sinuses, releasing enzymes to neutralize the bacteria.
•   ❖ The pain and swelling were intense, but they were part of the healing process. I
    later understood that the facial pressure I felt was due to the buildup of immune cells and
    fluid in my sinus cavities. My immune system was responding by increasing blood flow
    and sending immune cells to the site of infection — a natural inflammatory reaction, though
    it made me feel worse before I felt better.
•   ❖ I supported my recovery by combining medicine with immune-friendly habits. I
    took steam inhalation twice daily, stayed hydrated with warm fluids, consumed foods rich
    in vitamin C and zinc, and made sure to get enough sleep. I also stayed away from dust,
    used a humidifier at night, and practiced good hygiene to avoid secondary infections — all
    of which helped my immune system do its job more effectively.

    the pain faded, and the fever subsided. While the medications helped, I genuinely believe
    my immune system was the main warrior — identifying the infection, remembering how
    to fight it, and gradually restoring balance inside my body.
•   ❖ A few months later, I noticed something incredible: my body responded faster
    during cold seasons. Whenever I felt the onset of flu or sinus pressure, the symptoms
    didn’t escalate like before. I recovered quickly, and the infections were milder. That’s when
    I realized that this entire experience had become part of my immune memory. My immune
    system had learned from the previous battle and was now more efficient in fighting off
    similar infections.
•   ❖ This taught me how important immune memory is in building long-term resistance.
    The first battle was tough — it involved inflammation, blood, pus, and direct medical
    intervention — but now, my body seems better equipped. Memory cells in my immune
    system recognize the pathogens more quickly and initiate a stronger, faster response,
    protecting me before the infection becomes serious.
•   ❖ Today, I manage my health differently because of that experience. I avoid dusty
    environments, wear a mask in polluted areas, wash my hands regularly, and clean my
    bedding frequently. I also listen more closely to my body’s early signals and take
    preventive steps before an infection gets worse. I no longer ignore persistent flu symptoms,
    and I approach my health with more awareness and respect.
•   ❖ In the end, my journey through nasal sinusitis was more than just a painful episode
    — it was a lesson. A lesson in patience, in the power of immune defense, and in the value
    of timely treatment. My body didn’t just survive the infection — it adapted, learned, and
    grew stronger. And today, I carry that experience with me not as a weakness, but as a sign
    of how resilient our immune systems truly are when supported the right way.

SHORT QUESTIONS
   1. Tcr and bcr?
(TCR) is a protein complex found on the surface of T cells, or T lymphocytes,
BCR is a transmembrane protein on the surface of a B cell.
                                   OR
The main difference between BCR and TCR is that BCR binds directly to the
antigen surface, whereas TCR recognizes antigenic peptides with MHC molecules.
   2 Endogenous antigens?
Endogenous antigens induce immune response in the form of generation of
antibodies. The example of endogenous antigens induced cytotoxic
hypersensitivity include erythroblastosis fetalis.
3. Secondary lymphoid organs
These are the lymphoid tissues which are involved in providing the specific
immune response. These tissues are located distantly from central lymphoid tissues
that’s why are also called as peripheral lymphoid tissues.
4. Adjuvants and their effects on……..??
Adjuvants (from Latin adjuvare, to help) are substances that, when mixed with an
antigen and injected with it, enhance the immunogenicity of that antigen. And their
effects are:
• Antigen persistence is prolonged. • Co-stimulatory signals are enhanced. • Local
inflammation is increased. • The nonspecific proliferation of lymphocytes is
stimulated.
5. Name two drugs of hemolytic anemia??
Granulocytopenia & thrombocytopenia.
6. Characteristics of antibody?
Self / non-self-discrimination, Memory and Specificity.
7. Secondary lymphoid organs?

     The lymph nodes, spleen, and various mucosal associated lymphoid tissues
(MALT) such as gut associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) are the secondary (or
peripheral) lymphoid organs
8. Monoclonal antibodies usage?
Usage in prevention, diagnosis & treatment of disease. Typing of various tumors
e.g Leukemia, Immunohistochemistry of solid tumors and. Use in Fluorescence
Activated cell sorting (FACS)

9. Three component names of coagulation system? This system has three
   pathways, I didn’t get the three components……
The coagulation system is defined as a cascade of proteolytic reactions that lead to
the formation of a fibrin clot, It consists of three pathways: extrinsic, intrinsic,
and common, each involving specific factors.

10. Three names of immune responses? Or the question may be Three types of
    immune responses
Nonspecific responses, specific responses, Active Immunity and passive immunity

11. Domains in immunoglobulin structures?

  Light Chain:

   •   Variable Domain (VL)
   •   Constant Domain (CL)

  Heavy Chain:

   •   Variable Domain (VH)

   •   Constant Domains (CH1, CH2, CH3, and sometimes CH4

12. Tumor specific and tumor associated antigens.
 Tumor specific transplantation antigens these antigens are unique to tumor
cells. These are not expressed on normal cells. These antigens are responsible for
rejection of tumor by host immune system. In most cases, these antigens cannot be
easily identified
Tumor Associated transplantation antigens these antigens are expressed by both
tumor & normal cells in contrast to tumor specific transplantation antigens.
Various chemicals, UV radiations & viruses are responsible for expression of these
neo-antigens. Majority of these tumors are weakly immunogenic or non-
immunogenic
13. Freund’s adjuvants.
Freund’s Complete Adjuvants (FCA) Freund’s complete adjuvant (FCA) are
water-in-oil emulsion containing antigens with heat killed Mycobacterium
tuberculosis. These adjuvants have the ability to stimulate both humoral & cell
mediated immune response for antibody production. Freund’s Incomplete
Adjuvants These adjuvants are also water-in-oil emulsion containing antigens
without heat killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These are used as booster antigen
dose. These are used by mixing equal parts of the antigens.

14. Mechanism for the control of vesicular pathogen.
A subpopulation of Th cells, Th1 cells, is the primary defense against intracellular
pathogens that live within vesicles. Th1 cells recognize antigen from the pathogen
that are expressed on the surface of infected cells and release cytokines that
activate the infected cell. Once activated, the infected cell can then kill the
pathogen.
15. Note on classes of antibody.
Types of Immunoglobulins: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgD, and IgE
Antibodies, also known as immunoglobulins, are proteins produced by
lymphocytes as a result of interaction with antigens. Antibodies are a part of
the humoral immune of the adaptive immune system where each antibody
identifies a specific antigen and protects the body against it.

16. X-linked hyper IgM deficiency
This form of B-cell associated immunodeficiency has very high levels of IgM. As
a result, the levels of IgG & IgA get reduced. The underlying defect in this
condition is in class switching due to defect in CD40 ligand on CD4 T-cells. The
patients are susceptible to pyogenic infections like bacterial infections. This
condition can be treated with intravenous gamma globulins injections.

17. Mechanisms of immune evasion.
Mechanisms of Immune Evasion
 The strategy to escape from immune system is caused by different microbes
differently as follows a) Extracellular organisms These organisms usually
inactivate the humoral components of immune system b) Intracellular organisms
These organisms usually bypass the host immune system by inactivating
intracellular killing and other cell mediated immune mechanisms which are as
follows Antigenic Variation Microorganisms mutate their antigenic surface
molecules for immune-evasion which is called as antigenic variation. As a result,
there is not available longer protection by antibodies produced under previous
exposure of antigenic forms. There are following two forms of antigenic variations
• Antigenic shift This is the major form of change in antigenic structure of antigen
as a result the new strains of microbes are generated • Antigenic drift This is the
minor form of antigenic variation within the same strain for example influenza
(Flu) virus exhibits both antigenic shift and drift for pandemic and seasonal flu
respectively. Similarly, bacteria like E.coli, Neisseria gonorrhea and Salmonella
typhimurium also exhibit antigenic drift.

PREPARED BY BT GIRL’S

                                       CHAPTER # 21
What is immunodeficiency?

The deficiency or failure of immune system is called as immunodeficiency. It is a state of
complete absence of immunity or effective immune response. There are defects regarding
generation of immune reactivity against infectious agents like bacteria & virus etc. There is
no immune response against transformed cells like tumours or malignancy.

Who are immunodeficient patients?

The persons having immunodeficiency are also called as immunocompromised patients
because there is increased vulnerability for opportunistic infections in addition to other
forms of infections. As there is decrease surveillance against tumours so more chances of
getting tumours are there in immunodeficient patients.

How many categories are classified of Immunodeficiency?

Immunodeficiency is classified into two main categories based on mode of acquiring

   1. Primary Immunodeficiency
   2. Secondary Immunodeficiency

Explain the Classification of Immunodeficiency?

Primary Immunodeficiency
Primary immunodeficiency is basically the inherited or congenital defects of the immune
system. These defects can be either in specific or non-specific immune systems. Primary
immunodeficiency diseases can occur in individuals of any age. These are classified based on
the site of lesion in the developmental or differential pathway of immune system. The
chances of susceptibility to variety of infections get increased in this kind of
immunodeficiency. The nature of infection depends on the kind of immunodeficiency. There
are more than 400 primary immunodeficiencies. Some are relatively common, while others
are quite rare. Some affect a single cell or protein of the immune system and others may
affect two or more components of the immune system.

PREPARED BY BT GIRL’S

Secondary Immunodeficiency
This kind of immunodeficiency is not congenital in nature in contract to primary
immunodeficiency. This state of immunodeficiency is associated with infections for example
AIDS. There is also association of aging factor like hypo-cellularity in bone marrow.
Malignancies for example Leukaemia and Myeloma are also linked with secondary
immunodeficiency. Furthermore, other metabolic disorder like diabetes and renal
malfunction etc. are also linked with secondary immunodeficiency. The most common
secondary immune deficiencies are caused by aging, malnutrition, certain medications and
some infections, such as HIV.

Write down the kinds of Primary immunodeficiency?

Primary immunodeficiency can be of two kinds

Immunodeficiency in specific immune system
Those conditions due to defects of the adaptive immune system in which defence is carried
out in a more specific manner by T-cells and antibody producing B-cells. This kind of
immunodeficiency is due to defects in stem cell differentiation.

Immunodeficiency in Non-Specific immune system

Those fewer common conditions with defects in the innate immune system, a system of
cells and mechanisms that defend the host from infection in a non-specific manner.

Write down the important disease of immunodeficiency in specific immune system in
Primary Immunodeficiency?

Followings are the important disease of immunodeficiency in specific immune system

Reticular dysgenesis
It is either complete absence or severe deficiency of lymphocytes & granulocytes in blood
due to decrease differentiation of bone marrow stem cells.
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
This disorder is due to the involvement of lymphoid stem cells. There is complete absence of
T & B cell immunity. The patients suffering from SCID are susceptible to variety of bacterial,
viral, mycotic & protozoan infections.

DiGeorge Syndrome
This is the disorder of T-lymphocytes due to congenital thymic aplasia or hypoplasia. This
condition is highly immunodeficient as live vaccines also cause infections in the patients
suffering from DiGeorge syndrome.
X-linked hypo gammaglobulinemia
This kind of immunodeficiency is due to functional disorder of B-Lymphocytes. Such patients

PREPARED BY BT GIRL’S

are highly susceptible to recurrent bacterial infections.
IgA deficiency
There is deficiency of IgA in this disorder as a result individuals are susceptible to mucosal
surface infections like GIT, eye & nasopharynx.
Selective IgG deficiency
In this kind of immunodeficiency, there is selective deficiency of IgG which leads towards
hyper IgM immunodeficiency.

Write down the important disease of immunodeficiency in Non-Specific immune system in
Primary Immunodeficiency?

Followings are the important conditions which are linked with immunodeficiency in non-
specific immune system
Cyclic Neutropenia
There is low number of circulating neutrophils in the blood which cause recurrent bacterial
infections among such patients.
Chronic Granulomatous disease (CGD)
This kind of immunodeficiency is due to defects in phagocyte functions.
Complement deficiency
There is deficiency of complement proteins in this kind of immunodeficiency. Patients
suffering from such disorder are susceptible to infections particularly Neisseria.

What is AIDS?
Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). This condition is caused by a virus called as
human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). This condition is initiated through an initial infection
with influenza like illness. Further, the disease progress with other defects in immune
system leading towards severe immunodeficiency. The patients get severe opportunistic
infections like tuberculosis. Moreover, the chance of getting tumour also increased. AIDS is
linked with abnormalities in circular lymphocytes. AIDS patients have also increased
susceptibility to various following tumours

   •   Kaposi sarcoma
   •   Burkitt’s lymphoma
   •   Primary central nervous system lymphoma

Write down the mode of transmission of AIDS?

For AIDS, HIV infection is transmitted by following two modes

PREPARED BY BT GIRL’S

Horizontal transmission

35: Interleukins:
They are mediators between leucocytes
36: Chemokine:
They are responsible for leucocytes migration
37: Cytokines function as cascade signaling in the form of cytokine network.
38: mRNA
For cytokines are short lived.
39: What is Redundancy?
It is due to the nature of cytokine receptors.
40: Different cells can respond to same cytokine due to:
Structural similarities
41: Cytokine response in how many ways:
Three ways

42: what is Autocrine :
Effect on same cell which secrete cytokine
43: Paracrine:
Effect on nearby cells to cells which secrete cytokine
44: Endocrine:
Effect on distant cells through circulation
45: Cytokines categorized on which basis:
Two basis
46: On basis of source cell what are Monokines?
It produced by mononuclear phagocytic cells e.g. Interferon gamma & Interleukin
(IL- 1) from macrophages & Monocytes.
47: On basis of source cell what Lymphokines?
Produced by activated lymphocytes e.g. IL-3, IL-4 & IL-5
48: On basis of source cell what Interleukins?
They are mediators between leucocytes e.g. IL-1, IL-
10& IL-18
49: On basis of source cell what Chemokine’s?
They are responsible for leucocytes migration e.g. IL-8
50: Types of cytokine on basis of function:
1: Cytokines which act for innate (non-Specific) immune system e.g. TNF- α,
IL-1, Il 10 etc.
2: Cytokines which act for Adaptive (Specific) immune system e.g. Il- 2,IL-4 &
IL-5
51: What are Tumor Necrosis Factor-Alpha (TNF-α) :
It is produced by activated macrophages in response to microbes or their products
for example lipopolysaccharides (LPS) of gram negative bacteria. It acts a
mediator of acute inflammation. It recruits neutrophils and macrophages at the site
of infection either by stimulating endothelial cells to secrete adhesion proteins or
by secreting chemokines. Moreover, TNF-a induces fever and acute phase proteins
in host.
52) IL-1
This is also an inflammatory cytokine as like TNF-a. It is produced by activated
macrophages. Furthermore, it also help to activate T-cells.
53) IL-10
It is an inhibitory cytokine which inhibits the cytokine production of cytokines
from macrophages.
54) IL-12
This cytokine is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. It enhances the
cytolytic activity of cytotoxic T-cells

55) Type I interferon
This class of interferon include Interferon α & β. These inhibit viral replication in
cells by increasing the expression of class I MHC which in turn make them
susceptible to cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CTL).
56) IFN-γ
It is produced primarily by Th1 cells. It enhances the cytolytic activity of NK cells
by induction of class I & II MHC molecules.
57) Chemokines
These are chemotactic cytokines produced by many leucocytes. These recruits
inflammatory cells at site of infection for an inflammatory response.
58) Which cytokines which act primarily for Adaptive (Specific) immune system?
1) IL-2
It is produced by T-helper (Th) cells but Cytotoxic T-cells (Tc) also produced it in
lesser extent. It stimulate B-cell division. It can also activate NK cells and
monocytes. Moreover, IL-2 acts on T-cells in autocrine manner.

2) IL-4
IL-4 is produced by macrophages and Th2 cells. It promotes the development of
Th2 from naïve T-helper (Th) cells. The Differentiated Th2 cells result in the
production of antibodies. IL-4 also involves in the class switching of antibody into
IgE
3) IL-5

IL-5 is produced by Th2 cells. It promotes the development of B-cells and
eosinophils. It also activates mature eosinophils.
4) Tumor Growth Factor (TGF)-β

TGF- β is produced by T cells and many other cells types. It acts as inhibitory
cytokine which inhibits the proliferation of T-cells and activation of macrophages.
It also acts on neutrophils and endothelial cells to block the effects of pro-
inflammatory cytokines.
59) What are three phases of Immuno-regulation ?

1) Recognition phase

2) Activation Phase

3) Effector Phase

60) What is Immune Evasion?
All the strategies used by pathogenic organisms and tumor cells to evade host
immune’s system are called as immune evasion mechanisms.
61) What is mechanism of immune evasion?
The strategy to escape from immune system is caused by different microbes
differently as follows
a) Extracellular organisms
These organisms usually inactivate the humoral components of immune system

b) Intracellular organisms
These organisms usually bypass the host immune system by inactivating
intracellular killing and other cell mediated immune mechanisms
62) What is antigenic variation?

Types of active immunization vaccines:
Active immunization is the induction of immunity after exposure to an antigen, requiring
antigenic exposure. It occurs naturally or artificially, leading to antibody development and
memory response. The immune system generates antibodies slowly, providing long-term
immunity without pre-made antibodies in the host's serum.
Types: or Examples: Active immunization vaccines include live attenuated vaccines (e.g., MMR,
varicella), inactivated vaccines (e.g., polio, hepatitis A), subunit vaccines (e.g., hepatitis B,
HPV), conjugate vaccines (e.g., Hib), toxoid vaccines (e.g., tetanus, diphtheria), and mRNA
vaccines (e.g., COVID-19).

What is Opsonization?
Opsonization is the enhancement of the phagocytic process where pathogens are marked for
ingestion by phagocytes. Opsonins, such as immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM) and complement
proteins, bind to the bacterial surface, facilitating neutrophil or macrophage phagocytosis
through opsonin receptors like Fc and complement receptors.

The structure of TCR
The T-cell receptor (TCR) is a heterodimer surface receptor composed of two equal-length
chains (α and β). Each chain has a constant (C) and variable (V) region, with hypervariable
regions for specificity. TCRs have a short cytoplasmic tail, transmembrane region, and disulfide
bridge.

Characteristics of immunoglobulin:
Immunoglobulins (Ig) are antibodies produced by plasma cells, composed of two heavy and two
light chains forming a Y-shaped molecule. They have variable regions for antigen binding, and
constant regions for effector functions. Classes include IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, and IgD, each with
specific roles and functions.

Parts of secondary lymphoid system?
 The secondary lymphoid system includes structures where lymphocytes become activated and
initiate adaptive immune responses. Key parts of this system are:
1. Lymph Nodes: A=Filter lymph fluid, b=Sites for antigen presentation and lymphocyte
activation.
2. Spleen: A= Filters blood, B= Red pulp: Removes old red blood cells, c= White pulp: Immune
responses to blood-borne antigens.
3. Tonsils: A= Located at the throat and nasal passages. B=First line of defense against inhaled
or ingested pathogens.
4. Appendix: A=Contains lymphoid tissue. B= Plays a role in gut immunity.

Complement System:
The complement system is a group of proteins that enhance the immune response. These proteins
can directly attack pathogens, promote phagocytosis, and contribute to the inflammatory
response. Among complement proteins, some proteins have the ability to bind with
immunoglobulin molecules while some are involved in binding on the membrane component of
various immune cells.

Endogenous & exogenous antigen difference?
Endogenous and exogenous antigens are two main types of antigens that the immune system
recognizes and responds to:
Endogenous Antigens:
    Origin: Generated within the body's cells.
    Produced within the cell, presented by MHC Class I, and targeted by CD8+ T cells.
    Examples: Viral proteins produced inside infected cells, tumor antigens from cancerous
     cells, and normal cellular proteins presented during routine maintenance.
Exogenous Antigens:
    Origin: Enter the body from the external environment.
    presented by MHC Class II, and targeted by CD4+ T cells.
    Examples: Bacteria, fungi, parasites, pollen, and toxins.

Activation of B-cell receptor?
B-cells are activated when there is high concentration of antigen for example in case of bacteria
the lipopolysacchrides antigens exist in greater quantity. B-cell activation occur after binding of
antigen to a surface molecule which is known as B-cell receptor. Afterward there is bypassing of
the early part of the biochemical pathway mediated by specific antigen receptor. Cross linking of
immunoglobulin receptor occur due to repeating determinants on antigenic structure. As a result
the transformation of B-cells occur into plasma cell for immunoglobulin secretion.

Active / passive immunization?
1= Active immunization: It is the induction of immunity after exposure of host to antigen. In this
case, antigenic exposure is mandatory. Active immunization can occur naturally by exposing to
microbe or other antigen when there is no prior exposure before the entry of antigen. In this form
of immunization, immune system develops antibodies against the microbe after its exposure.
This process of antibodies generation is considered slow.
2= Passive immunization: It is the induction of active humoral immunity. In this kind of
immunization, antibodies are mandatory. Passive immunization can occur naturally by transfer
of maternal antibodies to fetus through placenta. However, the artificial induction can be done by
injecting gamma globulins from other individuals or animals to host.

Adaptive immune system?
    Response is antigen-dependent
    There is a lag time between exposure and maximal response
    Antigen-specific
    Exposure results in immunologic memory
    Specific
    Second line of Defense
    Needs to be activated

What are cytokines?
• Diverse group of non-antibody proteins • Act as mediators between cells • Initially these were
considered as products of immune cells • Also considered to act as mediator for immune cells •
Also produced from non-immune cells & mediators for them. • Used as biological response

modifier for treatment of various diseases • Cytokine is a general term but more specific term
used according to their cell of origin.

What are monoclonal antibodies?
The antibodies which are produced from a single antibody producing B-cell are called as
monoclonal antibodies. These antibodies also able to bind with single and unique antigen binding
sit (epitope). Monoclonal antibodies mainly consist of single subtype of IgG for example IgG1,
IgG2 & IgG3.

#Topic 85

CD3 complex Structure & Function

The CD3 stands for Cluster of differentiation 3. This structure is present adjacent to TCR. This is
basically the transducing element of TCR. It exists as a complex form which is composed of five
following proteins (as shown in fig.9.2), that’s why it is also called as CD3 complex

   1. One Gamma(γ)

   2. One delta(δ)

   3. Two Epsilon (ε)

   4. Two Zeta (ζ)

Figure 9.2: The structure of CD3 complex

The CD3 complex is considered as invariant proteins means with conserved regions without
variability. It has no role in determining the specificity of T-Cell. However, it is necessary for
surface expression of TCR during development of T-cell. This has very important role in
transducing signals from T-cell surface receptor to interior of cell which is called as Signal
transduction. This transduction signals arise after engaging of antigen with TCR in association
with MHC complex.

#Topic 86

Cell Surface Molecules involved in T-Cell & Other Interaction

The interface between antigen presenting cell (Target Cell) and T-lymphocyte occur for mounting
a strong immune response against antigen. This interaction between TCR & MHC molecules are
not so strong and called as immunological synapse. In this immunological synapse, the cell surface
molecules on T-cells & their interacting molecule on antigen presenting cells are involved. T-cells
also express co-receptor for MHC molecule (e.g CD8 & CD4). Moreover, the expression of
supporting molecules are increased by the action of cytokines released from either T-cells or
antigen presenting cells. The increased expression of supporting molecules for making
immunological synapse strong are called as modulators of immune system. In addition to these
molecules, some molecules are also required for T-cell activation. For the activation of T-cells
following two signals are required

    •    Signal 1 is generated after engagement of TCR with Antigen/MHC complex

    •    Signal 2 is generated after engagement of supporting molecules with their corresponding
         ligands

For signal 2, the co-stimulatory molecules are also required for activation of T-cells e.g C28 is a
co-stimulatory molecule on T-cell surface & its ligand exists on APC which is known as B7-1. If
there is lack of co-stimulation, then there is no activation of T-cells occur and this process is called
as cellular anergy. For the full activation of T-cells, the engagement of Immunological synapse is
mandatory. As a result the antigen presenting cells (APC) must possess & present peptides to T-
cells.

#Topic 87

Accessory Molecules

The interaction between TCR on T-cells & antigen/MHC complex on APC is considered as weak
for mounting a strong immune response. In order to stabilize this interaction, there is the need of
additional molecules in addition to TCR & antigen/MHC which are called as accessory molecules.
These molecules are invariant molecules and have no role in determining the specificity of T-cells.
However, these accessory molecules can modulate the immune system in either positive or

molecules are according to their function.

Followings are the important accessory molecules (Fig 9.3 & 9.4)

Chapter# 1: Overview of the Immune System as the
Body’s main Defense Mechanism
Introduction to basic Terminology
Immunity

It is the resistance to disease specifically infectious disease or infections.

Immune system

The collection of cells, tissues and molecules that mediate resistance to infection is called as
immune system

Immune response

The coordinated reaction of cells and molecules of immune system against infectious microbes is
termed as immune response

Immunology

The study of immune system & immune response with physiological function to prevent infections
and to eradicate established infections inside body

Infectious vs Non-infectious diseases

Infections

These are contagious, transmittable and communicable diseases which are caused by an invading
or infectious agent. The infectious agent is a foreign particle to body’s immune system. These can
be microbes like bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. That’s’ why infections can be bacterial,
viral, fungal and parasitic in nature for example typhoid is a bacterial infection while hepatitis is a
viral infection. Infections can be transmitted from one individual to other through various ways
like aerosols, blood and also from mother to fetus.

Non-infections

These are non-communicable and non-contagious diseases in contrast to infections. These are not
caused by purely by an infectious or invading agents but these agents can be a secondary reasons
for such kind diseases for example in case of most of cancers are caused by various infectious
agents secondarily. Non-infectious diseases are generally considered as metabolic disorders in
which there is any defect in the metabolism of any bio-molecule for example diabetes mellitus is
a carbohydrate metabolic disorder. These disease also have the tendency to transmit genetically
from one generation to other.

Role of Immune System

The importance of the immune system for health is evident by the conditions when individual
suffering from various fetal diseases in case of defective immune response. The most important
function of immune system is to protect the body from the attack of infectious or invading
microbes. If the individual’s immune system does not work properly then the chances of acquiring
infections also increased for example in case of Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
This indicates the importance of immune system for defending against infections. Similarly, there
is also very significant role of immune system in organ transplantation. Immune response act as a
barrier for successful organ transplantation as immune system recognizes and responds to tissue
graft and newly introduced proteins. Immune system also provides surveillance against tumors and
cancers. Moreover, for treatment of cancers immunotherapy also have good implications. The
products of immune system like antibodies are highly specific molecules for detecting any kind of
molecules. Likewise, antibodies are widely used for developing immunologic approaches for
laboratory testing in clinical medicine and research.

Types of Immunity

For providing defense against various infections, there are two important types of immunity

   1) Innate or non-specific Immunity
   2) Adaptive or specific immunity

Innate Immune System

It is a non-specific immune system which serve as the first line of defense against pathogens.
Innate immune system is readily available all the time in order to fight against microbes. Moreover,

this form of immune system is also antigen independent and non-specific. There is immediate
maximal response from innate immune system against attacking pathogens. Innate immune system
lack in memory against the various forms of infections

Adaptive Immune System

It is considered as the second line of protection against various pathogen specifically. It needs
activation after invasion by pathogen in a very specific manner. This system is antigen dependent
with specificity. For the activation of adaptive immune system, it needs lag time for fully activation
during which naive cells become active after differentiation and activation. Adaptive immune
system has the unique attribute of memory against specific nature of pathogens.

Components of Innate Immune system

Innate immune system is the first line of defense against invading pathogens. It is comprised of
following three important components or barriers

   1) Anatomical barriers
   2) Humoral (Secretory) barriers
   3) Cellular barriers

Anatomical barriers

Those defensive mechanisms which are related to various structures of body are the part of
anatomical barriers. These are composed of three major arms including

   a) Mechanical arm
   b) Chemical arm
   c) Biological arm

Mechanical Arm

It is comprised of various mechanical defense by different structure of body for example like skin
which is considered as a physical barrier for protection against invading agents. Similarly, the
lining epithelium membrane of various body cavities like GIT & skin in the form of squamous
epithelium which has the property of desquamation in order to get rid of infectious agent.
Moreover, the peristalsis and cilliary movements of GIT also protect from the ingested

microorganisms Flushing actions of tears and saliva also make the mechanical arm of anatomical
barriers. The mucus lining of GIT and respiratory tract also has the trapping action for providing
protection against invading pathogens

Chemical arm

It is composed of various chemicals which effect on the invading pathogens for providing
protection for example skin contains various fatty acids which don’t allow the organisms to grow
on it. Similarly, tears and nasal secretions carry various enzymes like lysozymes & phospholipases
for degradation of invading pathogens by breaking their cell wall. Likewise, defensins also have
antimicrobial actions against pathogens in GIT and lungs. Moreover, low pH of GIT & sweat
secretions inhibit the growth of pathogenic microorganisms. However, lungs also contain
surfactants which increase the process of phagocytosis for potential pathogen by the process of
opsonization.

Version 1
1. Introduction

Pakistan remains one of the last countries where wild poliovirus circulates. Eradication efforts
hinge on two vaccines—the oral polio vaccine (OPV) and the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)—
whose complementary immune profiles underpin both individual protection and community‐
level defense.

2. Immunological Mechanisms

OPV delivers live-attenuated poliovirus strains directly to the gastrointestinal tract. These
attenuated viruses replicate in the gut epithelium and elicit strong secretory IgA responses, which
intercept wild poliovirus at its entry point and reduce fecal–oral spread. Conversely, IPV is a
killed-virus injectable that cannot replicate; it stimulates systemic IgG production, which
circulates through the bloodstream to neutralize any poliovirus before it invades neural tissue and
causes paralysis.

3. Herd Immunity Role

OPV’s capacity for secondary transmission—shedding attenuated virus that can immunize
contacts—serves as a powerful driver of herd immunity in densely populated, low-sanitation
areas. IPV, while unable to propagate itself, fills individual immunity gaps by ensuring that each
vaccinated child has circulating neutralizing antibodies, thus reinforcing community protection
against outbreaks and vaccine-derived strains.

4. Pakistan’s Immunization Strategy

Under the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), Pakistan conducts multiple annual
OPV campaigns (e.g., National Immunization Days) targeting every child under five years of

age. In 2017, a single IPV dose at 14 weeks of age was introduced into the routine schedule to
bolster systemic immunity. This dual approach balances OPV’s transmission-blocking strengths
with IPV’s safety profile, aiming to reach the >95 percent coverage threshold recommended by
WHO.

5. Challenges and Conclusion

Persistent rumors about vaccine safety, security‐related access barriers in tribal regions, and
cold-chain breakdowns undermine coverage. Overcoming these obstacles requires engaging
trusted community leaders, strengthening logistics (including solar-powered refrigeration), and
integrating polio activities with other maternal–child health services. By aligning OPV’s mucosal
immunity and IPV’s systemic defense with robust outreach, Pakistan can convert vaccine
efficacy into eradication success.

Version 2
Context

Wild poliovirus persists in Pakistan, necessitating a vaccination regimen that leverages both
OPV and IPV. Each vaccine triggers distinct arms of the immune system to block infection and
transmission.

OPV: Gut-Level Immunity

Administered orally, OPV contains live-attenuated poliovirus that colonizes the intestinal
mucosa. This replication induces high levels of secretory IgA, which form the first line of
defense against wild virus entry and replication. Furthermore, vaccinated children shed the
attenuated strain, inadvertently immunizing their contacts and amplifying community immunity.

IPV: Circulatory Defense

IPV is given by injection and consists of chemically inactivated poliovirus particles. Although
IPV does not replicate in the gut, it elicits a potent systemic IgG response. These antibodies
circulate in the blood, neutralize invading poliovirus, and prevent its progression to the central
nervous system, thereby averting paralytic disease.

Synergistic Herd Impact

OPV’s indirect spread is critical in achieving herd immunity in Pakistan’s high-density settings,
where direct coverage may falter. IPV complements this by guaranteeing that vaccinated
individuals cannot develop paralytic polio, even if exposed. Together, they reduce both
transmission potential and disease burden.

  Inbox for paid LMs Work & Project Handing at M.Kashif(03064963933)

National Strategy & Barriers

Pakistan’s EPI framework schedules four OPV doses—at birth and at 6, 10, and 14 weeks—plus
supplementary mass OPV campaigns. IPV was added in 2017 at 14 weeks to strengthen systemic
immunity. Despite these measures, misinformation campaigns, violent conflict in border
districts, and unreliable cold chains continue to create immunity gaps. Addressing these
challenges through local influencer engagement, improved data-driven microplanning, and
integrated health outreach is vital to closing the last transmission chains.

Version 3
Overview

Eradicating polio in Pakistan depends on harnessing two vaccines—OPV and IPV—that engage
different immunological pathways yet together build a resilient population barrier against the
virus.

Gut-Centered Defense via OPV

OPV’s live-attenuated virus replicates in the gut lining, stimulating mucosal immunity
dominated by secretory IgA antibodies. This localized response prevents wild poliovirus from
taking hold and, through community shedding, extends protection indirectly to unvaccinated
peers—a phenomenon crucial for herd immunity.

Bloodstream Barrier via IPV

IPV, an injectable formulation of killed virus, cannot spread but provokes systemic IgG
antibodies. These immunoglobulins patrol the bloodstream, neutralizing any poliovirus before it
can invade motor neurons. IPV thus provides a fail-safe against paralysis and counters the
emergence of vaccine-derived poliovirus strains.

BT302 - Immunology

Lesson 1 : Overview of Immune System:

Please Click here to dowload the PPT file

Immunity

It is defined as the state of protection from infectious disease

It has both a less specific and more specific component.

   1. The less specific component, innate immunity, provides the first line of defense against
      infection.
   2. The specific component, adaptive immunity, does not come into play until there is an
      antigenic challenge to the organism.

The Immune system

Immune system is the defense system that has evolved to protect animals from invading
pathogenic microorganisms and cancer.

It is able to generate an enormous variety of cells and molecules capable of specifically
recognizing and eliminating an apparently limitless variety of foreign invaders.

Immune response

An immune response can be divided into two related activities

   1. Recognition
   2. Response

Immune recognition is remarkable for its specificity. The immune system is able to recognize
subtle chemical differences that distinguish one foreign pathogen from another.

Furthermore, the system is able to discriminate between foreign molecules and the body’s own
cells and proteins.

Once a foreign organism has been recognized, the immune system recruits a variety of cells and
molecules to mount an appropriate response, called an effector response, to eliminate or
neutralize the organism.

In this way the system is able to convert the initial recognition event into a variety of effector
responses, each uniquely suited for eliminating a particular type of pathogen.

Later exposure to the same foreign organism induces a memory response, characterized by a
more rapid and heightened immune reaction that serves to eliminate the pathogen and prevent
disease

Immunology

The discipline of immunology grew out of the observation that individuals who had recovered
from certain infectious diseases were thereafter protected from the disease. The Latin term
immunis, meaning “exempt,” is the source of the English word immunity, meaning the state of
protection from infectious disease.

Reference

Kuby Immunology, 6th Edition, Authored by Kindt, Goldsby and Osborne, Chapter 1, Pages 1, 4

Lesson 2 : Infections vs Non-Infections:

Please Click here to dowload the PPT file

Infectious disease

Infectious diseases are caused by pathogenic micro-organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi or
parasites. These micro-organisms are contagious.

Examples of infectious diseases include the common cold, COVID-19, SARS and tuberculosis.

Non-infectious disease

Non-infectious diseases are not caused by pathogens and therefore cannot be spread from one
person to another. Instead, non-infectious diseases are caused by factors such as genetics,
malnutrition, environment and lifestyle.

Examples of non-infectious diseases include cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and epilepsy.

Differences between an infectious and non-infectious disease

1. Infectious diseases are communicable, non-infectious diseases are not

Infectious diseases are contagious, meaning that a person can contract the illness if they are
exposed to carriers of the disease. For example, COVID-19

Non-infectious diseases, are non-communicable, meaning they cannot be transmitted through
exposure to a carrier. Instead, they appear due to factors such as gene mutations, malnutrition,
environmental toxins and lifestyle.

2. Infectious diseases are caused by the transmission of a pathogen

Infectious diseases are transmitted from person-to-person through the transfer of a pathogen such
as bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites.

A non-infectious disease cannot be transmitted through a pathogen.

3. Prevention strategies for infectious disease focuses on stopping the spread

Prevention strategies for infectious disease focus on isolating individuals who have the disease to
protect the broader population, and vaccinating against known strains to prevent transmission.

4. Preventative measures for non-infectious diseases are lifestyle and contextually-focused

Preventative measures for non-infectious disease are focused on lifestyle choices and patterns.
You can reduce your risk of contracting Type 2 diabetes, for example, by maintaining a healthy
weight, exercising regularly and consuming a balanced diet.

Not all non-infectious diseases, however, can be prevented. Some can develop as a result of an
individual’s genetic history, lifestyle or age.

Reference

https://www.childfund.org.au/stories/what-is-the-difference-between-an-infectious-and-non-
infectious-disease/

Sometimes the immune system fails to protect the host adequately or misdirects its activities to
cause discomfort, debilitating disease, or even death.

There are several common manifestations of immune dysfunction:

   •   Allergy and asthma
   •   Graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease
   •   Autoimmune disease
   •   Immunodeficiency

Graft rejection and graft-versus-host disease

When the immune system encounters foreign cells or tissue, it responds strongly to rid the host
of the invaders. However, in some cases, the transplantation of cells or an organ from another
individual, although viewed by the immune system as a foreign invasion, maybe the only
possible treatment for disease. Because the immune system will attack and reject any
transplanted organ that it does not recognize as self, it is a serious barrier to this potentially life-
saving treatment.

An additional danger in transplantation is that any transplanted cells with immune function may
view the new host as nonself and react against it. This reaction, which is termed graft-versus-host
disease, can be fatal.

Subjective bt302 final 2025

1. Immune System and Lungs

The lungs have specialized immune defenses to protect against infections:

       Mucociliary clearance: Mucus traps pathogens, and cilia move them out.
       Alveolar macrophages: Phagocytose inhaled pathogens.
       IgA antibodies: Provide mucosal immunity.
       Cytokines and chemokines: Regulate immune responses.

2. V(D)J Recombination

V(D)J recombination is the genetic process by which B and T cells generate diverse antigen
receptors. It involves:

       Variable (V), Diversity (D), and Joining (J) gene segments.
       RAG-1 and RAG-2 enzymes that cut and rearrange DNA.
       Essential for adaptive immunity (unique antibodies and T-cell receptors).

3. B Cell Without T Cell

B cells can function without T cells in T-independent antibody responses, but:

       They mainly produce IgM antibodies (low affinity).
       They don’t form memory cells effectively.
       T-cell help (T-dependent response) is needed for class switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE.

4. What Is Affinity Maturation?

Affinity maturation is the process by which B cells produce antibodies with increased binding
strength to an antigen. It occurs in:

       Germinal centers of lymph nodes and spleen.
       Somatic hypermutation (SHM) alters antibody genes to improve binding.
       High-affinity B cells survive and differentiate into plasma and memory cells.

5. X-Linked Immunodeficiencies

These are genetic disorders that primarily affect males. Examples:

      X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA) – B cells fail to mature.
      X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) – Defective T and B cell
       function.
      Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) – Phagocytes can't kill bacteria properly.

6. Three Names of Accessory Molecules

Accessory molecules help immune cell communication. Examples:

   1. CD4 – Helps T-helper cells recognize MHC-II antigens.
   2. CD8 – Helps cytotoxic T-cells recognize MHC-I antigens.
   3. CD28 – Provides co-stimulation for T-cell activation.

7. Genetic Drift and Genetic Shift

      Genetic drift: Small random mutations in viruses (e.g., flu virus changes yearly).
      Genetic shift: Large changes due to gene exchange (e.g., new flu pandemics).

8. Importance of the Immune System

      Protects against infections (bacteria, viruses, fungi).
      Removes dead or abnormal cells (prevents cancer).
      Prevents autoimmunity by distinguishing self from non-self.

9. How Parasites Are Killed (Mast Cells and Eosinophils)

      Mast cells release histamine to increase inflammation and recruit immune cells.
      Eosinophils release toxic granules (e.g., major basic protein) to kill large parasites like
       helminths.

10. Examples of Endogenous Antigens

Endogenous antigens are produced inside cells. Examples:

      Viral proteins in infected cells.
      Tumor-specific antigens in cancer cells.
      Self-antigens (sometimes trigger autoimmunity).

11. Types of Graft Rejection According to Time

      Hyperacute rejection (Minutes to hours) – Due to pre-existing antibodies.
      Acute rejection (Days to weeks) – T-cell mediated.
      Chronic rejection (Months to years) – Slow tissue damage due to fibrosis.

12. Mechanisms of Immune Evasion

Pathogens escape immune detection using:

      Antigenic variation (e.g., flu virus changes surface proteins).
      Inhibiting MHC presentation (e.g., herpes virus).
      Producing immune-suppressive molecules (e.g., HIV).

13. Domains of Immunoglobulins

Antibodies have distinct structural regions:

      Variable domain (Fab region) – Binds antigen.
      Constant domain (Fc region) – Interacts with immune cells.
      Hinge region – Provides flexibility.

14. How Immune System Responds Against Intracellular Pathogens

Intracellular pathogens (e.g., viruses, some bacteria) trigger:

      Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+) – Kill infected cells.
      Interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β) – Inhibit viral replication.
      Natural killer (NK) cells – Destroy infected cells lacking MHC-I.

15. V(D)J Recombination Sequences

      V(D)J recombination generates T-cell receptors (TCRs) and B-cell receptors (BCRs).
      Recombination signal sequences (RSS) guide DNA rearrangement.
      RAG-1 and RAG-2 enzymes mediate recombination.

16. Lymphocyte Recirculation

Lymphocytes continuously move between blood, lymph, and tissues to detect infections.

      T-cells home to lymph nodes to encounter antigens.
      Memory cells circulate for rapid response to reinfection.
      Chemokines and adhesion molecules direct movement.

17. What Is Tumor-Specific and Tumor-Associated Antigens?

      Tumor-specific antigens (TSA): Found only on cancer cells (e.g., mutated p53).
      Tumor-associated antigens (TAA): Found on both cancer and normal cells but at higher
       levels in cancer (e.g., AFP in liver cancer).

1. Usage of Monoclonal Antibodies

Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-made molecules engineered to act like natural
antibodies. They are used in:

      Medical treatments: Cancer therapy (e.g., Rituximab), autoimmune diseases (e.g.,
       Infliximab), and infectious diseases.
      Diagnostics: Pregnancy tests, ELISA, and Western blot.
      Research: Identifying specific proteins in cells or tissues.

2. Defects in IgA Deficiency

IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency. It can lead to:

      Increased respiratory and gastrointestinal infections.
      Higher risk of allergies and autoimmune diseases.
      In some cases, it may be asymptomatic.

3. Types of Graft Rejection According to Time

Graft rejection occurs when the recipient's immune system attacks a transplanted organ. The
types based on time are:

      Hyperacute rejection (Minutes to hours) – Due to pre-existing antibodies.
      Acute rejection (Days to weeks) – Caused by T-cell response.

Chapter# 1: Overview of the Immune System as the
Body’s main Defense Mechanism
Introduction to basic Terminology

Immunity

It is the resistance to disease specifically infectious disease or infections.

Immune system

The collection of cells, tissues and molecules that mediate resistance to infection is called as
immune system

Immune response

The coordinated reaction of cells and molecules of immune system against infectious microbes is
termed as immune response

Immunology

The study of immune system & immune response with physiological function to prevent infections
and to eradicate established infections inside body

Infectious vs Non-infectious diseases

Infections

These are contagious, transmittable and communicable diseases which are caused by an invading
or infectious agent. The infectious agent is a foreign particle to body’s immune system. These can
be microbes like bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. That’s’ why infections can be bacterial,
viral, fungal and parasitic in nature for example typhoid is a bacterial infection while hepatitis is a
viral infection. Infections can be transmitted from one individual to other through various ways
like aerosols, blood and also from mother to fetus.

Non-infections

These are non-communicable and non-contagious diseases in contrast to infections. These are not
caused by purely by an infectious or invading agents but these agents can be a secondary reasons
for such kind diseases for example in case of most of cancers are caused by various infectious
agents secondarily. Non-infectious diseases are generally considered as metabolic disorders in
which there is any defect in the metabolism of any bio-molecule for example diabetes mellitus is
a carbohydrate metabolic disorder. These disease also have the tendency to transmit genetically
from one generation to other.

Role of Immune System

The importance of the immune system for health is evident by the conditions when individual
suffering from various fetal diseases in case of defective immune response. The most important
function of immune system is to protect the body from the attack of infectious or invading
microbes. If the individual’s immune system does not work properly then the chances of acquiring
infections also increased for example in case of Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
This indicates the importance of immune system for defending against infections. Similarly, there
is also very significant role of immune system in organ transplantation. Immune response act as a
barrier for successful organ transplantation as immune system recognizes and responds to tissue
graft and newly introduced proteins. Immune system also provides surveillance against tumors and
cancers. Moreover, for treatment of cancers immunotherapy also have good implications. The
products of immune system like antibodies are highly specific molecules for detecting any kind of
molecules. Likewise, antibodies are widely used for developing immunologic approaches for
laboratory testing in clinical medicine and research.

Types of Immunity

For providing defense against various infections, there are two important types of immunity

   1) Innate or non-specific Immunity
   2) Adaptive or specific immunity

Innate Immune System

It is a non-specific immune system which serve as the first line of defense against pathogens.
Innate immune system is readily available all the time in order to fight against microbes. Moreover,

this form of immune system is also antigen independent and non-specific. There is immediate
maximal response from innate immune system against attacking pathogens. Innate immune system
lack in memory against the various forms of infections

Adaptive Immune System

It is considered as the second line of protection against various pathogen specifically. It needs
activation after invasion by pathogen in a very specific manner. This system is antigen dependent
with specificity. For the activation of adaptive immune system, it needs lag time for fully activation
during which naive cells become active after differentiation and activation. Adaptive immune
system has the unique attribute of memory against specific nature of pathogens.

Components of Innate Immune system

Innate immune system is the first line of defense against invading pathogens. It is comprised of
following three important components or barriers

   1) Anatomical barriers
   2) Humoral (Secretory) barriers
   3) Cellular barriers

Anatomical barriers

Those defensive mechanisms which are related to various structures of body are the part of
anatomical barriers. These are composed of three major arms including

   a) Mechanical arm
   b) Chemical arm
   c) Biological arm

Mechanical Arm

It is comprised of various mechanical defense by different structure of body for example like skin
which is considered as a physical barrier for protection against invading agents. Similarly, the
lining epithelium membrane of various body cavities like GIT & skin in the form of squamous
epithelium which has the property of desquamation in order to get rid of infectious agent.
Moreover, the peristalsis and cilliary movements of GIT also protect from the ingested

microorganisms Flushing actions of tears and saliva also make the mechanical arm of anatomical
barriers. The mucus lining of GIT and respiratory tract also has the trapping action for providing
protection against invading pathogens

Chemical arm

It is composed of various chemicals which effect on the invading pathogens for providing
protection for example skin contains various fatty acids which don’t allow the organisms to grow
on it. Similarly, tears and nasal secretions carry various enzymes like lysozymes & phospholipases
for degradation of invading pathogens by breaking their cell wall. Likewise, defensins also have
antimicrobial actions against pathogens in GIT and lungs. Moreover, low pH of GIT & sweat
secretions inhibit the growth of pathogenic microorganisms. However, lungs also contain
surfactants which increase the process of phagocytosis for potential pathogen by the process of
opsonization.

Chapter # 13: Cytokines
Overview about Cytokines

                                                 Page 1 of 26

Created By Muhammad Hassan

03482688820
Cytokines belong to diverse group of non-antibody proteins which act as mediators between
cells. Initially, these proteins were considered as products of immune cells. More importantly,
these were also considered to act as mediators for immune cells. Later on, it was also found that
these are also produced from non-immune cells and served as mediators too. Cytokines are used
as biological response modifier for treatment of various diseases. In general, cytokine is a
general term but it can be more specific term which is used according to their cell of origin as
follows

   •   Monokines

These are produced by mononuclear phagocytic cells.

   •   Lymphokines

These are produced by activated lymphocytes.

   •   Interleukins

These are the mediators between leucocytes

   •   Chemokines

These are responsible for leucocytes migration and inflammatory process

Cytokines usually perform their functions as cascade signaling in the form of a network which is
termed as cytokine network. Their functions are for enhancing their effects of other cytokines in
an additive or synergistic manner. Moreover, these act for suppressing the effects of other
cytokines in an opposing or antagonistic way. Cytokines are not as preformed proteins like
antibodies. These are produced by gene transcription as needed because mRNA for cytokines are
short lived in nature. Furthermore, the individual cytokine can act on many cells of the host
which is termed as pleotropic response of cytokines.

Mechanism of acting of Cytokines

                                                                                     Page 2 of 26

Created By Muhammad Hassan

03482688820
Cytokines act through specific receptors present on various cells. These are considered as
redundant in nature. The redundancy of cytokines is due to the nature of cytokine receptors. The
complex interaction between host’s cells and cytokines occur through cytokine network.
Different cells can respond to same cytokine due to structural similarities among cytokine
receptors (Fig.13.1). The cytokine signaling is flexible which can have both protective and
damaging effects. Similarly, thes can also influence the synthesis of other cytokines.

Figure 13.1: The structure of various cytokine receptors

Cytokines bind to specific receptors with high affinity and respond in following three ways

   1. Autocrine

These effect on same cells which secrete the cytokine

   2. Paracrine

In this way, the cytokines effect on nearby cells of cytokine secreted cells.

   3. Endocrine

Through this way, the cytokines effect on distant cells through circulation.

                                                                                         Page 3 of 26

Created By Muhammad Hassan

03482688820
Categories of Cytokines

Cytokines are categorized on following two basis

  I.          Their source of origin

 II.          Their functions

       I. Categories based on source cells

Followings are the categories of cytokines on the basis of their source of origin

       i)        Monokines

As the name indicates, these are produced by mononuclear phagocytic cells for example
Interferon gamma and Interleukin (IL-1) from macrophages & Monocytes

       ii)       Lymphokines

These are produced by activated lymphocytes for example IL-3, IL-4 & IL-5.

       iii)      Interleukins

These are mediators between leucocytes for example IL-1, IL-10& IL-18.

       iv)       Chemokines

These are responsible for leucocytes migration for example IL-8.

       II. Based on functions

On the basis of functions, cytokines are categorized into following two categoryies

       a) Cytokines which act for Innate (non-Specific) immune system e.g TNF-α, IL-1, Il-10 etc

       b) Cytokines which act for Adaptive (Specific) immune system e.g Il-2,IL-4 & IL-5

Cytokines of Innate Immune System

These cytokines which act primarily for innate (non-Specific) immune system. These are as
follows

                                                                                      Page 4 of 26

Created By Muhammad Hassan

03482688820
   1) Tumor Necrosis Factor-Alpha (TNF-α)

It is produced by activated macrophages in response to microbes or their products for example
lipopolysaccharides (LPS) of gram negative bacteria. It acts a mediator of acute inflammation. It
recruits neutrophils and macrophages at the site of infection either by stimulating endothelial
cells to secrete adhesion proteins or by secreting chemokines. Moreover, TNF-a induces fever
and acute phase proteins in host.

   2) IL-1

This is also an inflammatory cytokine as like TNF-a. It is produced by activated macrophages.
Furthermore, it also help to activate T-cells.

   3) IL-10

It is an inhibitory cytokine which inhibits the cytokine production of cytokines from
macrophages.

   4) IL-12

This cytokine is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. It enhances the cytolytic activity
of cytotoxic T-cells

   5) Type I interferon

This class of interferon include Interferon α & β. These inhibit viral replication in cells by
increasing the expression of class I MHC which in turn make them susceptible to cytotoxic T-
lymphocytes (CTL).

   6) IFN-γ

It is produced primarily by Th1 cells. It enhances the cytolytic activity of NK cells by induction
of class I & II MHC molecules.

   7) Chemokines

These are chemotactic cytokines produced by many leucocytes. These recruits inflammatory
cells at site of infection for an inflammatory response.
